intro.caption: Lesson 9-4 — using two-variable equations to solve problems. The last supply ship of the season can drop just ONE cargo pod before storm season. Oxygen, water or food? The crew has to predict which supply runs low first, and prove it. Three gates and a boss decide what drops.

balloons.t: One pod. One kind of cargo. Show me with equations what we need most. And Pebble may NOT order rocks.
We ration oxygen now: 4 canisters a day. So c = 4d. And we have 60 canisters left.

pages.caption: Takoda used the equation backwards. In c = 4d, the 60 canisters is c, not d. Ask: which letter does this number belong to?

balloons.t: Substitute means swap the letter for a number. Days go in for d.

pages.ch: Chapter 2 · How Long Will It Last?

balloons.t: 60 is canisters, Takoda. We need to SOLVE for the days.
Food comes in whole crates. 12 meal packs each. We need 100 packs.
Bip. (Screen: Rocks also come in whole crates.)
The recycler uses 15 liters a day. The tank has 180.
Oxygen or water? Pick the one that runs out first.
BEEP-BEEP-BEEP! (Screen: Water delivered. Also, I found a rock in the pod.)

win.caption: To use an equation, substitute the number into the right variable. To find the input, solve it with the inverse operation. When things come whole, "at least" means round up. Then justify the choice with the math.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Substitute
gates.prompt:
The colony rations oxygen to 4 canisters each day. Let d = days and c = canisters used. The equation is c = 4d.
Days, dCanisters used, c
14
28
520
hints: Conceptual: substitute means replace a letter with a number. A number of days replaces d; a number of canisters replaces c.
Procedural: 4d means 4 × d. Write c = 4 × (days), then multiply.

steps: Practice: the water recycler uses 15 liters a day: w = 15d.
For 3 days, substitute 3 for d: w = 15 × 3.
w = 45. In 3 days the recycler uses 45 liters.
worked.q: Using w = 15d, how many liters in 4 days?

items.label: Canisters used in 6 days, c =

fb.msg: 1.5 is 6 ÷ 4, the equation backwards. 6 is days, so it replaces d: c = 4 × 6.
4d means 4 × d. Writing 4 next to 6 makes forty-six.

items.fbDefault: Replace d with 6 in c = 4d, then multiply.

items.q: Which shows substituting 9 days into c = 4d?

options.fb: That puts 9 in for c, the canisters. 9 is a number of DAYS, so it replaces d.
4d means 4 times d, not 4 plus d.
4d means 4 × d. Writing 4 next to 9 makes forty-nine.

gates.pass: 24 canisters for 6 days, 36 for 9 days. Esme writes it on the storeroom door.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Solve
gates.prompt: The storeroom has 60 oxygen canisters. The colony uses them by c = 4d. How many days will they last?
hints: Conceptual: 60 is a number of canisters, so it replaces c. Then d is the unknown you solve for.
Procedural: write 4d = 60. Undo "times 4" with the inverse operation: divide both sides by 4.

steps: Practice: the water recycler uses w = 15d. The tank has 90 liters.
90 is liters, so it replaces w: 15d = 90.
Divide both sides by 15: d = 90 ÷ 15 = 6 days. Check: 15 × 6 = 90. ✓

items.q: Which equation finds how many days 60 canisters last?

options.fb: That's Takoda's mistake: the equation backwards. 60 is canisters (c), not days (d).
Each day uses 4 canisters, so there are FEWER days than canisters. Divide, don't multiply.
Adding does not undo "times 4." Use the inverse operation, division.

fb.msg: 240 is 4 × 60, the equation backwards. You treated 60 as days. Solve 4d = 60 instead.

gates.pass: 15 days of oxygen, not 240. Takoda says 240 "felt right." Leilani says feelings are not math.

gates.title: Gate 3 · At Least
gates.prompt: Each food crate holds 12 meal packs. The crew needs at least 100 meal packs. Let n = number of crates: 12n ≥ 100. Crates only come whole.
hints: Conceptual: "at least 100" means 100 or more. Find the smallest whole number of crates that gets there. A part of a crate cannot be sent.
Procedural: divide 100 by 12. If it is not a whole number, try the whole numbers next to it: multiply each by 12.

steps: Practice: each water jug holds 10 liters, and the crew needs at least 45 liters: 10j ≥ 45.
4 jugs hold 40 liters, not enough. 5 jugs hold 50 liters. At least 5 jugs.
worked.q: Each tank holds 20 L. The crew needs at least 50 L. At least how many tanks?

items.label: At least how many crates?
items.aria: least number of whole food crates for 100 meal packs

fb.msg: 100 ÷ 12 is 8⅓, but crates come whole. 8 crates are not enough, so round UP.
100 ÷ 12 is about 8.33, but crates come whole. Round UP to have at least 100 packs.
8 crates × 12 = 96 packs. That is less than 100, so it is not enough.
1200 is 12 × 100, the equation backwards. 100 is meal packs, not crates.

items.fbDefault: Try whole numbers of crates: how many packs do 8 crates hold? 9 crates?

items.q: Why is the answer a whole number of crates and not 8⅓?

options.t: 8⅓ is fine. Just cut a crate open.
options.fb: The ship sends whole crates. A third of a crate cannot be ordered.

options.t: Round 8⅓ to 8, the nearest whole number.
options.fb: 8 crates hold 96 packs, less than 100. "At least" means round UP.

options.t: Crates come whole, and 8 crates hold only 96 packs.

options.fb: 9 × 12 = 108, not 100. The statement is false, but 108 is still at least 100.

gates.pass: 9 crates: 108 meal packs, at least 100. Leilani checks it off. Pebble's rock crate is denied.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Send the Drop
gates.prompt: Oxygen: 60 canisters last 15 days (Gate 2). Water: the recycler uses w = 15d liters, and the tank has 180 liters. Choose the cargo, and justify it.
hints: Conceptual: compare supplies by how many DAYS each lasts, not by the size of the numbers. Liters and canisters are different units.
Procedural: 180 is liters, so it replaces w. Solve 15d = 180. Then compare with 15 days of oxygen.

steps: Practice: power cells are used by p = 3d, and there are 24 cells. Solve 3d = 24: d = 8 days.
To last 10 days, the colony needs p = 3 × 10 = 30 cells.
So it needs at least 30 − 24 = 6 more cells.
worked.q: Using w = 15d, how many liters for 2 days?

items.label: Days the water lasts, d =
items.aria: days that 180 liters of water last

fb.msg: 2700 is 15 × 180, the equation backwards. 180 is liters (w), so solve 15d = 180.

items.fbDefault: Substitute 180 for w, then divide both sides by 15.

items.q: What should the pod carry, and why?

options.fb: 15 days is LONGER than 12. The supply that runs out first is the one to send.

options.t: Water, because it runs out in 12 days and oxygen lasts 15.

options.fb: Canisters and liters are different units. Compare the DAYS each supply lasts.

options.t: Water, because 180 is the biggest number.
options.fb: Right cargo, wrong reason. A big number of liters does not mean it runs out first. Compare days: 12 vs 15.

items.label: To have water for 20 days, at least how many MORE liters?
items.aria: extra liters of water needed for 20 days

fb.msg: 300 liters is ALL the water for 20 days. The tank already has 180.
8 is the extra DAYS. Each day uses 15 liters.
480 is 300 + 180. Subtract what the tank already has.

items.fbDefault: Find w for 20 days with w = 15d. Then subtract the 180 liters already in the tank.

gates.pass: Decision: water. 12 days is less than 15, and the pod needs at least 120 more liters. Okafor sends the order.

journal.heading: Lesson 9-4 — what the supply drop taught us
rows: Replace a letter with a number that matches it. 6 days replaces d in c = 4d: c = 4 × 6 = 24.
To find the input, undo the operation. 4d = 60, so d = 60 ÷ 4 = 15 days.
When things come whole, round UP. 12n ≥ 100 gives 8⅓, so at least 9 crates.
Compare in the same unit. Water lasts 12 days, oxygen 15, so water drops first.
Using the equation backwards: 60 canisters is c, not d. 4 × 60 = 240 days was never true.
journal.quote: "I solved for rocks. The answer was: more rocks." — Pebble (via Idris's screen)

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 9-4 (Apply Two-Variable Relationships to Solve Problems) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: substituting into a two-variable equation, solving for the independent variable with an inverse operation, "at least" predictions that round up, and justifying a decision with the math.
standards: Use variables to represent two quantities that change in relationship to one another; write an equation for the dependent variable in terms of the independent variable; analyze the relationship using graphs and tables
